subject: FREN
course_description: A survey of literary and cultural creations from the Francophone world, with a special emphasis on Africa, the Caribbean, and South East Asia.
course_notes: FREN 391R. Indigeneity in the French-speaking World. Lyna Ami Ali / Tuesdays and Thursdays 2:30-3:45PM Content: What does it mean to be from one place? Who gets to belong, and who gets to decide? How have colonization, slavery, migration, and displacement complicated our understanding of indigeneity? And what forms of solidarity emerge between communities shaped by colonialism and migration? This course explores indigeneity in the French-speaking world through French-language texts, film, and art, focusing on Indigenous communities in Africa, Oceania, and the Caribbean. In French colonial contexts, indigène became a discriminatory political and legal category under the Code de l¿Indigénat, distinguishing colonized peoples from French citizens. Through case studies of Touareg, Pygmy, Kalinago, Kabyle and Kanak communities, we will examine how these communities have reclaimed and reshaped these colonial categories through the French language. The course also considers how indigenous identities are erased and others recreated, concluding with global perspectives on migration and indigeneity, asking how movement across borders transforms our understanding of home, belonging, and place. Throughout, students will engage in constant dialogue with indigenous scholars, and non-academic communities in the Atlanta and Macon areas. The course will be conducted entirely in French. Texts may include: Abdelwaheb Sefsaf, Kaldûn, (2023, Théâtre de Sartrouville, 140 min.) Guy Cabort Masson, La Mangrove mulâtre (1986) Isis Labeau-Caberia, La Prophétie Des Soeurs-Serpents (2022) Kateb Yacine, Louise Michel et La Nouvelle-Calédonie (2004) Louisa Yousfi, Rester barbare (2022) Mouloud Mammeri, La Colline Oubliée (1952) Sarah Maldoror, Monangambeee (1968, Angola, Algeria, 16 min.)
